sources.text:
Identify plants in an image, classify their species, and analyze their health, end to end, with inference fast enough to serve over an API.

Sarah built the whole system on her own.

An end-to-end computer vision pipeline: YOLO detects the plants, and CLIP classifies them and analyzes their health. A GPU-accelerated FastAPI backend serves the pipeline, optimized for low-latency inference, and the system is deployed on AWS EC2.

Only an overview of this project is recorded. For details beyond it, ask Sarah directly.

The system was built end to end and deployed on an AWS EC2 GPU instance.

Images arrive from the field into object storage, and the system needs to tell, for each one, whether there are weeds and how severe they are. The results feed a dashboard that shows the health of the plants (PHI). The system had to run continuously on a machine with no GPU.

There was no local GPU, so a heavy model was not practical, neither to train nor to run continuously. The images come from field conditions, with noise, changing light and small leaves.

The team built a whole smart agriculture system. Sarah built this part, weed detection, entirely on her own, as one component of that system.

Images from the field land in MinIO. The `weed-detector` service fetches each image, runs MobileNetV3 on it, computes bounding boxes, severity and coverage, and writes the results to PostgreSQL. A dashboard reads these results to show the health of the plants (PHI).

**The model:** a pretrained MobileNetV3, with the last layer replaced by a new layer of two classes, weeds and no weeds. This keeps what the model already learned and trains only the final decision.

**Training and evaluation:** the data was split into train, validation and test sets. Loss and accuracy were tracked on every epoch to check for overfitting, and accuracy was measured on the test set at the end. The model was then also checked on new images from MinIO, to see that it generalizes to real data.

The service runs in Docker, on CPU.

**MobileNetV3 classification instead of UNet segmentation.** Sarah started with UNet, a segmentation model that marks weeds pixel by pixel. It performed well, but without a local GPU, training took an unrealistic amount of time, and it is heavy to run. The task did not need a full pixel mask, only whether weeds are present and how severe they are. MobileNetV3 is built for running without a GPU: it is light, fast on CPU, keeps the Docker image lean, and was accurate enough for the task.

The model was accurate enough for an operational task, with high and stable results on the test set, and it held up on new images from MinIO. A Data / ML Engineering Bootcamp at VAST Data in 2025, as an internship. The team built a smart agriculture system. Sarah built two components of it entirely on her own: weed detection, and image embeddings with similarity search.

- An end-to-end weed detection pipeline with Python, PyTorch and MobileNetV3: fetching images from MinIO, running inference, and storing the results in PostgreSQL.
- An image embedding system with CLIP / ViT-mini, publishing vectors to Kafka and loading them into pgvector for similarity search and analytics.
- Containerizing backend and AI services in Docker, for reproducible development and deployment.

- `weed-detection-pipeline`: weed detection on CPU with MobileNetV3, after UNet proved impractical without a GPU.
- `clip-embeddings-kafka`: image embeddings with CLIP / ViT-mini, through Kafka into pgvector, with similarity search on request.

AI Engineer at Ainsof Capital in 2026, working remotely. Sarah was the sole engineer of a production data-governance platform, and owned it end to end, from architecture design through launch.

The platform manages reliable information. Every piece of information has a source, a trust score, and a full record of who changed what and when. When two sources contradict each other, the system detects it and sends it to a person to check, instead of deciding on its own.

The product and its business domain are not described here.

- Designing the claims-based data model: every fact is sourced, trust-scored, auditable and checked for conflicts.
- Building the PostgreSQL layer: schemas, migrations, row-level security, triggers, RPC functions, optimistic concurrency and idempotency keys.
- Building the governance API that the data center works against.
- Performance work on the API.
- Building a machine translation pipeline on the Claude API, behind a human approval gate.
- Building the 28-screen governance center and the bilingual, offline-first travel PWA.

A separate team built the scraping that pulls data from websites, which is one of the sources of claims.

- `claims-trust-model`: the claims-based data model, with trust, conflicts and human review.
- `postgres-rls-backbone`: the PostgreSQL layer, with three schemas, row-level security and safe concurrent writes.
- `api-latency-582-to-40`: cutting API latency from 582ms to 40ms per request.
- `human-gated-translation`: machine translation with the Claude API that never overwrites a person's edit.
- `governance-center-pwa`: the 28-screen governance center and the bilingual offline-first PWA.

sources.text:
A Data / ML Engineering Bootcamp at VAST Data in 2025, as an internship. The team built a smart agriculture system. Sarah built two components of it entirely on her own: weed detection, and image embeddings with similarity search.

- An end-to-end weed detection pipeline with Python, PyTorch and MobileNetV3: fetching images from MinIO, running inference, and storing the results in PostgreSQL.
- An image embedding system with CLIP / ViT-mini, publishing vectors to Kafka and loading them into pgvector for similarity search and analytics.
- Containerizing backend and AI services in Docker, for reproducible development and deployment.

- `weed-detection-pipeline`: weed detection on CPU with MobileNetV3, after UNet proved impractical without a GPU.
- `clip-embeddings-kafka`: image embeddings with CLIP / ViT-mini, through Kafka into pgvector, with similarity search on request.

AI Engineer at Ainsof Capital in 2026, working remotely. Sarah was the sole engineer of a production data-governance platform, and owned it end to end, from architecture design through launch.

The platform manages reliable information. Every piece of information has a source, a trust score, and a full record of who changed what and when. When two sources contradict each other, the system detects it and sends it to a person to check, instead of deciding on its own.

The product and its business domain are not described here.

- Designing the claims-based data model: every fact is sourced, trust-scored, auditable and checked for conflicts.
- Building the PostgreSQL layer: schemas, migrations, row-level security, triggers, RPC functions, optimistic concurrency and idempotency keys.
- Building the governance API that the data center works against.
- Performance work on the API.
- Building a machine translation pipeline on the Claude API, behind a human approval gate.
- Building the 28-screen governance center and the bilingual, offline-first travel PWA.

A separate team built the scraping that pulls data from websites, which is one of the sources of claims.

- `claims-trust-model`: the claims-based data model, with trust, conflicts and human review.
- `postgres-rls-backbone`: the PostgreSQL layer, with three schemas, row-level security and safe concurrent writes.
- `api-latency-582-to-40`: cutting API latency from 582ms to 40ms per request.
- `human-gated-translation`: machine translation with the Claude API that never overwrites a person's edit.
- `governance-center-pwa`: the 28-screen governance center and the bilingual offline-first PWA.
